# Abstract

The southern Himalayan arc encompassing Nepal and Bhutan (183.712 km², comprising 2.452 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells) constitutes one of the most formidable ecological and altitudinal gradients on Earth. Rising precipitously from the subtropical alluvium of the Gangetic Terai and the Duars across temperate intramontane valleys to the glaciated summits of the Great Himalaya, this mountainous domain mediated commercial, religious and demographic exchanges between South Asia and the Tibetan plateau. Reconstructed across four physiographic and historical divisions under INDUS, regional population expanded from 15k terminal Pleistocene foragers in 10000BC during early post-glacial recolonisation to 85k in 3000BC with the establishment of pastoralism, buckwheat cultivation and polished stone celt technologies. Following the introduction of iron metallurgy and terraced wet-rice farming, population climbed to 320k in 500BC and 680k in 200AD, when classical urbanisation crystallised in the lacustrine basin of the Kathmandu Valley under the Licchavi dynasty. Intensification of farmer-managed irrigation canals, the development of trans-Himalayan trade routes and the political consolidation of the Newar Malla kingdoms, the Khasa Malla empire of the western Karnali basin and the Drukpa theocracy in Bhutan drove population to 1,15M in 800AD, 1,65M in 1200AD, 2,25M in 1500AD and 2,95M in 1700AD. By the culmination of Gorkha imperial unification and the Treaty of Sugauli in 1816AD, aggregate population attained 3,65M inhabitants (yielding an average density of 19,87 persons per 100 km²). Demographic weight remained concentrated within the central hills and the Kathmandu basin, which accommodated 1,75M people (48% of the regional total; 31,38 persons per 100 km²), supported by multi-tiered craft metropolises at Kathmandu, Lalitpur and Bhaktapur [@Slusser1982NepalMandala; @Toffin1990Mythical]. The western Khasa valleys supported 766,5k inhabitants (21%; 12,38 persons per 100 km²), while the eastern Kirat hills housed 803k (22%; 29,45 persons per 100 km²) and the Bhutanese dzong valleys maintained 328,5k (9%; 8,49 persons per 100 km²). This historical demographic reconstruction combines 4.060 georeferenced settlement trajectories—exhibiting a tight Zipf rank-size distribution ($\alpha = 0,80$, $R^2 = 0,99$)—with epigraphic, genomic and architectural evidence to model twelve millennia of montane population dynamics.

# Background

## Physiographic Architecture and Altitudinal Zonation

The demographic geography of the central and eastern Himalayas is governed by an extreme vertical zonation that compresses tropical to alpine environments into horizontal spans of less than 150 km [@Coningham2021Urban; @Parajuli1999Agro]. In Nepal and Bhutan, four distinct longitudinal morpho-tectonic zones succeed one another from south to north:
1. The Terai and Duars lowlands: a low-gradient piedmont apron of Quaternary boulder fans (Bhabar) and fine alluvial silt terraces (Terai) sitting between 60 m and 300 m above sea level. Historically blanketed by dense malarial sal (*Shorea robusta*) jungle and tall elephant grass, this zone functioned as an ecological buffer that repelled permanent high-density settlement until eighteenth-century forest clearances [@Compagna2026Layered; @Kovacs2024Bengal].
2. The Sub-Himalayan Siwalik (Chure) ranges: low, fragile sandstone ridges rising to 1.200 m, dissected by dry river torrents and supporting seasonal pastoral grazing rather than extensive cultivation.
3. The Middle Hills (Pahad or Mid-Hills): a dissected upland belt ranging between 1.000 m and 3.000 m, framed by the Mahabharat Lekh to the south and the Great Himalaya to the north. Comprising tectonic depressions such as the Kathmandu and Pokhara valleys alongside deeply incised river valleys (the Karnali, Gandaki, Bagmati, Koshi and Manas systems), the Mid-Hills accommodated the vast majority of regional population through intensive terraced agriculture [@Parajuli1999Agro; @Shrestha2016Traditiona].
4. The Great Himalaya and Trans-Himalayan valleys: glaciated massifs exceeding 7.000 m, punctuated by high mountain passes (such as Kuti, Kerung, Mustang, Tremo La and Nathu La) leading onto the arid Tibetan plateau. Here, transhumant pastoralism, yak breeding and long-distance caravan trade predominated over arable farming [@Ling2016India; @GnecchiRuscone2018Unraveling].

Precipitation is heavily concentrated in the summer monsoon between June and September, varying from over 4.000 mm annually along the windward southern slopes of eastern Nepal and Bhutan to under 300 mm in rain-shadow basins such as Mustang and northern Dolpo [@Parajuli1999Agro]. This asymmetric moisture distribution dictated settlement placement, compelling highland societies to settle near perennial glacial streams where gravitational irrigation could support cereal cropping [@Shrestha2016Traditiona].

## Prehistoric Foundations and the Neolithic-Chalcolithic Horizon

During the terminal Pleistocene and early Holocene, archaeological evidence indicates sparse occupations by mobile hunter-gatherer bands exploiting microthermal woodland habitats in the Siwalik hills and the Mahabharat range [@Coningham2021Urban]. At 10000BC, regional population is estimated at 15k individuals (yielding an aggregate density of 0,08 persons per 100 km²), dispersed in rock shelters and seasonal river-terrace camps. The warming climatic conditions of the early Holocene optimum facilitated the colonisation of higher altitudinal zones.

Between 6000BC and 3000BC, the transition from foraging to food production was marked by the diffusion of cord-impressed pottery, polished stone axes (celt traditions) and domesticated cereals [@De2022Legacies]. In the mid-hill valleys of central Nepal and western Bhutan, early agriculturalists practised swidden cultivation of buckwheat (*Fagopyrum esculentum*), barley (*Hordeum vulgare*) and foxtail millet (*Setaria italica*), supplemented by the hunting of wild ungulates and the rearing of humped zebu cattle (*Bos indicus*), taurine cattle and domestic sheep [@De2022Legacies; @GnecchiRuscone2018Unraveling]. Population expanded to 85k by 3000BC (0,46 persons per 100 km²). Autosomal genetic markers and mitochondrial lineages indicate that this demographic base represented an ancient admixture between indigenous South Asian hunter-gatherers and incoming Tibeto-Burman populations migrating westward along the Himalayan crest [@GnecchiRuscone2018Unraveling; @Kraaijenbrink2014Linguistic].

The introduction of iron metallurgy and double-cropping during the first millennium BC spurred significant demographic growth, lifting population to 320k in 500BC (1,74 persons per 100 km²). In the central hills, semi-tribal Kirata confederacies consolidated sedentary village networks [@Hutt1984Nepali]. Concurrently, along the southern Terai margin, early urban polities emerged as part of the broader Gangetic Iron Age urbanisation, exemplified by the Shakya republic at Tilaurakot (Kapilavastu) and sacred pilgrimage centres at Lumbini and Ramagrama [@Coningham2021Urban; @Maskey2024Religious].

## Classical Urbanisation: The Licchavi Dynasty and Early Trans-Himalayan Trade

Between the fourth and eighth centuries AD, the Kathmandu Valley emerged as the political and economic nucleus of the central Himalayas under the Licchavi dynasty [@Toffin1990Mythical; @Subedi2024Conservati]. The drained bed of the ancient palaeo-lake of Kathmandu provided thousands of hectares of deep, fertile lacustrine sediment (*kalimati*) capable of sustaining intensive agriculture [@Coningham2021Urban]. Licchavi monarchs established an administrative apparatus grounded in Sanskrit epigraphy, Shaiva and Buddhist religious patronage and sophisticated hydraulic engineering [@Giri2026Cosmos; @Shrestha2016Traditiona].

Regional population grew to 680k in 200AD and 1,15M by 800AD. Licchavi urbanism was distinguished by three structural innovations:
1. Gravitational water architecture: builders constructed extensive brick-lined municipal conduits (*rajkulo*) that tapped mountain springs and diverted streamflow into stepped public stone spouts (*dhunge dhara* or *hiti*) and storage cisterns throughout urban quarters [@Shrestha2016Traditiona].
2. Corporate social institutions: the *guthi* system of endowed land trusts arose during this era, ensuring the perpetual maintenance of canals, temples, bridges and rest houses through agricultural revenues [@Subedi2024Conservati].
3. Commercial brokerage: following the unification of Tibet under the Yarlung dynasty in the seventh century AD, the Kathmandu Valley became the primary transit entrepôt linking northern India with Lhasa via the Kyirong and Nyalam passes [@Ling2016India; @Blackwell1996Incorporat]. Nepali merchants exported musk, copper vessels, wool and paper while handling trans-Himalayan currency flows.

## Mediaeval Florescence: The Malla Kingdoms, Khasa Empire and Drukpa Dzongs

The mediaeval era (800AD to 1700AD) witnessed profound institutional consolidation and settlement nucleation across both Nepal and Bhutan. Regional population expanded from 1,15M in 800AD to 1,65M in 1200AD, 2,25M in 1500AD and 2,95M in 1700AD.

In the Kathmandu Valley, the Malla dynasty oversaw the division of the basin into three rival sovereign city-states: Kantipur (Kathmandu), Lalitpur (Patan) and Bhadgaon (Bhaktapur) [@Toffin1990Mythical; @Sengupta2017Ruptured]. Each capital developed dense brick architecture, paved public plazas (*durbar* squares), multi-tiered pagoda temples and specialised quarters inhabited by Newar artisanal castes, such as the *sikami* woodcarvers of Bhaktapur [@Gosai2025Ethnograph; @Whitmarsh2022Darbar; @Glattli2021Conservati]. Outside the urban perimeters, every square metre of valley alluvium was sculpted into terraced fields irrigated by complex networks of communal feeder canals [@Parajuli1999Agro].

Simultaneously, in the western Karnali basin, the Khasa Malla empire established a sprawling highland realm between the eleventh and fourteenth centuries, ruled from Sinja in Jumla and Dullu in Dailekh [@Hutt1984Nepali]. The Khasa kings commanded trans-Himalayan trade routes to Lake Manasarovar and Mount Kailash in western Tibet, issuing stone inscriptions that document the early development of the Nepali language (*Khas Kura*) [@Hutt1984Nepali]. Following the dissolution of the Khasa empire in the late fourteenth century, western Nepal fragmented into two clusters of petty principalities: the Baise Rajya (twenty-two principalities) along the Karnali and the Chaubisi Rajya (twenty-four principalities) along the Gandaki [@Hutt1984Nepali].

In Bhutan, the introduction of Drukpa Kagyu Buddhism during the twelfth and thirteenth centuries transformed the agrarian landscape [@Ling2016India]. In the seventeenth century, Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal unified the disparate valley chiefdoms of western and central Bhutan into a centralised theocratic polity [@Ling2016India; @Compagna2026Layered]. The Zhabdrung instituted the dual system of religious and civil governance (*chho-sid-nyi*) and supervised the construction of monumental fortress-monasteries (*dzongs*) at strategic river junctions, including Punakha, Paro, Thimphu, Trongsa and Jakar [@Ling2016India]. These dzongs operated as combined administrative headquarters, military bastions and monastic colleges, concentrating grain reserves collected as agricultural tax from surrounding peasant valleys.

## Gorkha Expansion, Highland Unification and the Anglo-Nepalese War

During the mid-eighteenth century, Prithvi Narayan Shah, ruler of the small hill state of Gorkha in the central mid-hills, launched a systematic military campaign to conquer the fragmented principalities of Nepal [@Whitmarsh2022Darbar; @Kieniewicz2020Identifyin]. After imposing an economic blockade on the Kathmandu Valley, Gorkhali forces captured Kathmandu and Patan in 1768AD and Bhaktapur in 1769AD, establishing Kathmandu as the imperial capital of a unified Himalayan state [@Whitmarsh2022Darbar; @Sengupta2017Ruptured].

Gorkha expansion continued eastward across the Kirat hills to the Sikkim border and westward across the Chaubisi and Baise states into Kumaon and Garhwal, reaching the Sutlej River by the early nineteenth century [@Kieniewicz2020Identifyin; @Compagna2026Layered]. This expansion altered land tenure systems through the grant of *birta* (tax-free land grants) and *jagir* (land assignments to military officers), encouraging the clearance of mid-hill forests and the reclamation of lower river valleys for wet-rice farming [@Parajuli1999Agro].

This rapid expansion brought the Gorkha empire into direct conflict with the British East India Company along the ill-defined Terai borderlands, culminating in the Anglo-Nepalese War of 1814-1816 [@Kieniewicz2020Identifyin; @Compagna2026Layered]. Under the Treaty of Sugauli (1816AD), Nepal surrendered its conquests west of the Mahakali River and east of the Mechi River alongside large portions of the Terai, establishing the modern territorial limits of the kingdom. At this baseline benchmark, regional population reached 3,65M inhabitants across Nepal and Bhutan.

# Methodology

## Spatial Grid and Terrestrial Environmental Covariates

To model demographic distributions across 183.712 km² of mountainous terrain, INDUS establishes a spatial raster encompassing 2.452 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells. Each terrestrial cell is evaluated against environmental covariates:
- Altitudinal and slope penalties: penalising uninhabitable alpine terrain and permanent snowpack above 4.500 m, while concentrating settlement potential within temperate valley floors between 600 m and 2.200 m [@Coningham2021Urban].
- Fluvial proximity and irrigation suitability: evaluating distance to perennial river channels (the Karnali, Gandaki, Bagmati, Koshi and Manas systems) capable of sustaining gravitational canal diversions (*kulo*) [@Parajuli1999Agro; @Shrestha2016Traditiona].
- Alluvial soil suitability: weighting deep lacustrine clays in the Kathmandu basin and fertile river terraces (*tar*) across the mid-hills above stony mountain slopes.
- Malarial attenuation in lowlands: down-weighting the southern Terai and Duars prior to 1750AD to account for endemic hyperendemic malaria (*falciparum*), which restricted human habitation primarily to indigenous Tharu populations possessing genetic resistance [@Compagna2026Layered; @GnecchiRuscone2018Unraveling].

## Settlement Subtraction and Dasymetric Mid-Hill Allocation

To avoid double-counting population between nucleated urban centres and rural agricultural communities, 4.060 catalogued settlements (1.491 in the Kathmandu Valley and Central Pahad, 1.263 in Western Khasa Malla and Karnali, 880 in the Eastern Kirat Hills and Koshi Terai, and 426 in Bhutanese Valleys and Drukpa Dzongs) are anchored to their WGS84 geographic coordinates with longitudinal population trajectories. At each benchmark year, the aggregated population of active catalogued settlements within each sub-region is deducted from the sub-regional demographic envelope.

The residual rural population is then allocated across non-settled grid cells in proportion to environmental suitability weights. A two-pass boundary smoothing filter feathers transitions along sub-regional drainage divides, preventing step discontinuities across mountain ranges.

## Demographic Uncertainty Bounds and Benchmark Calibration

Each sub-regional and headline benchmark estimate incorporates an explicit symmetric uncertainty bound (+/- 8% across benchmark dates from 10000BC to 1816AD). At the 1816AD baseline, the regional total of 3,65M is bounded between 3,36M and 3,94M inhabitants. This range reflects variations across colonial cadastral returns, Gorkhali tax rosters and house-count multipliers [@Kieniewicz2020Identifyin; @Compagna2026Layered].

# Testing and Validation

## Geoarchaeological and Epigraphic Ground-Truthing

Validation of historical settlement distributions in the central Himalayas relies upon the extensive corpus of Sanskrit, Newari and Tibetan stone inscriptions (*shilapatra*) alongside stratified excavations across urban and sacred sites [@Coningham2021Urban; @Toffin1990Mythical; @Slusser1982NepalMandala]. Licchavi inscriptions catalogued from the fifth century AD onwards confirm municipal administrative boundaries (*grama*, *tala*, *dranga*) across the Kathmandu Valley, demonstrating that towns such as Lalitpur and Kathmandu supported dense populations organised into functional wards [@Toffin1990Mythical; @Subedi2024Conservati; @Slusser1982NepalMandala].

In the southern Terai, geophysical surveys and excavations at Shravasti, Tilaurakot and Lumbini confirmed fortified urban layouts with monumental brick ramparts, moats and orthogonal street grids dating from the mid-first millennium BC to the early centuries AD [@Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @Allchin1995Archaeology; @Coningham2021Urban]. At Sinja in western Nepal, archaeological investigations of the Khasa Malla capital revealed stone temple complexes, sculpted hero stones and extensive irrigation terracing along the Hima River, corroborating historical accounts of fourteenth-century imperial nucleation in the Karnali highlands [@Hutt1984Nepali].

## Agro-Ecological Carrying Capacity and Farmer-Managed Irrigation

Agrarian carrying capacity in the mid-hills was governed by the availability of perennial water for gravitational canal systems [@Parajuli1999Agro; @Shrestha2016Traditiona]. Research on farmer-managed irrigation systems demonstrates that indigenous stone-and-brushwood diversion weirs (*kulo*) achieved high hydraulic efficiency on steep hillside gradients [@Parajuli1999Agro]. In the Kathmandu basin, multi-cropping regimes combined winter wheat and mustard with transplanted monsoon rice, yielding sufficient grain surpluses to support an urban craft population exceeding 20% of the valley total [@Toffin1990Mythical; @Gosai2025Ethnograph].

During the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, the introduction and rapid diffusion of New World cultigens—principally maize (*Zea mays*), potatoes (*Solanum tuberosum*) and chillies—expanded the agricultural frontier onto marginal, rain-fed hillside soils (*bari*) that could not support irrigated rice [@Parajuli1999Agro]. This dietary expansion raised caloric yields across the mid-hills and the high valleys of Bhutan, underpinning the demographic acceleration observed between 1500AD (2,25M) and 1700AD (2,95M).

## Genomic Demography and Linguistic Stratigraphy

Recent genomic investigations provide biological constraints on demographic reconstructions across the southern Himalayan arc [@GnecchiRuscone2018Unraveling; @Kraaijenbrink2014Linguistic]. Genome-wide SNP and autosomal STR analyses reveal structured genetic diversity reflecting distinct waves of human migration:
- An ancient Tibeto-Burman ancestral component shared across Kirat, Sherpa, Tamang and Bhutanese populations, showing adaptations to high-altitude hypoxia through alleles in the *EPAS1* and *EGLN1* loci [@GnecchiRuscone2018Unraveling; @Kraaijenbrink2014Linguistic].
- An Indo-Aryan ancestral component concentrated among Khas (Brahmin, Chhetri) and Newar high-caste populations, reflecting continuous gene flow from northern India from the late first millennium BC onwards [@GnecchiRuscone2018Unraveling].

Linguistic stratigraphy mirrors these demographic layers [@Hutt1984Nepali]. The eastward expansion of Khas Kura (proto-Nepali) from the Karnali basin displaced or assimilated indigenous Tibeto-Burman dialects across the central hills, providing a shared administrative idiom that facilitated the political consolidation of the Gorkha state in the late eighteenth century [@Hutt1984Nepali; @Kieniewicz2020Identifyin].

## Source Ledger Ingestion and Four-Wave Saturation Audit

The INDUS source ledger for Nepal and Bhutan was assembled through a four-wave asymptotic ingestion protocol designed to eliminate spatial omission biases:
- Wave 1: Ingestion of official national census tables (including Census of India Table A-04, CBS Nepal and NSB Bhutan), imperial metropolis anchors and regional gazetteers, capturing 2.355 primary settlements [@ImperialGazetteer1908; @Bayly1983Rulers; @Slusser1982NepalMandala].
- Wave 2: Systematic extraction of sites from multi-repository archaeological corpora, ASI and heritage registers, Wikidata, OpenStreetMap, Zenodo site catalogues and epigraphic monographs, adding 1.137 localities [@Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @Allchin1995Archaeology; @Coningham2021Urban].
- Wave 3: Macro-calibrated pre-1800 *qasba* and *pargana* continuity backfills alongside foundation-year and chronological toponymy audits across early monastic foundations, pilgrimage shrines and frontier trading posts, incorporating 568 sites [@Habib1982Atlas; @Moosvi1987Economy; @Phuntsho2013HistoryBhutan].
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap sweeps and GeoNames homonym audits across sovereign borders, which yielded zero unaccounted settlements and confirmed complete asymptotic saturation (marginal gain 0%).

In total, 4.335 candidate records were audited: 4.060 were verified and included as primary catalogued settlements (1.491 in Kathmandu Valley and Central Pahad, 1.263 in Western Khasa Malla and Karnali, 880 in Eastern Kirat Hills and Koshi Terai, and 426 in Bhutanese Valleys and Drukpa Dzongs), while 275 were excluded (predominantly duplicate survey aliases within a 2,2 km spatial radius, homonyms and non-habitation ritual shrines).

# Results

## Long-Term Demographic Trajectory (10000BC to 1816AD)

The demographic evolution of Nepal and Bhutan across twelve millennia demonstrates steady long-term growth, accelerating markedly with classical urbanisation, mediaeval craft intensification and late eighteenth-century imperial unification (Figure \ref{fig:trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:benchmarks}).

## Epochal Trajectories across the Himalayan Arc

The demographic history of the region divides into five major historical epochs:

### Prehistoric Foraging and Highland Dispersal (10000BC to 3000BC)

During the terminal Pleistocene and early Holocene, small family bands occupied seasonal camps in the Siwalik foothills and lower river terraces, foraging for wild tubers, hunting mountain game and catching river fish. Population rose from 15k in 10000BC (0,08 persons per 100 km²) to 85k in 3000BC (0,46 persons per 100 km²). The introduction of domesticated zebu cattle and stone celts enabled the first semi-permanent clearings in the mid-hill temperate zone [@De2022Legacies; @GnecchiRuscone2018Unraveling].

### Iron Age Settlement and Early Polities (3000BC to 200AD)

Between 3000BC and 200AD, the adoption of iron tools accelerated forest clearance across the Mahabharat range and the upper Terai. Regional population expanded from 85k to 320k in 500BC and reached 680k by 200AD (3,7 persons per 100 km²). Along the Terai fringe, early urban centres connected to Gangetic trade networks flourished at Shravasti (45k peak in 300BC; 23,8k in 200AD), Tilaurakot (Kapilavastu, 18k peak in 300BC; 8k in 200AD) and Janakpur (18k peak in 300BC; 14k in 200AD) [@Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @Allchin1995Archaeology; @Coningham2021Urban]. In the hills, tribal lineages coalesced into permanent agrarian hamlets.

### Classical Licchavi Urbanisation (200AD to 800AD)

Between 200AD and 800AD, population expanded from 680k to 1,15M (6,26 persons per 100 km²). The Kathmandu Valley emerged as an urbanised oasis, anchored by Kathmandu (16k in 200AD, rising to 30k in 800AD), Lalitpur (18k in 200AD, rising to 26,6k in 800AD) and surrounding Licchavi settlements [@Slusser1982NepalMandala; @Toffin1990Mythical; @Subedi2024Conservati]. Licchavi rulers codified corporate institutions and tapped trans-Himalayan commerce, establishing monasteries and commercial wards along the Bagmati and Vishnumati rivers [@Slusser1982NepalMandala; @Shrestha2016Traditiona].

### Mediaeval Splintering and Agrarian Expansion (800AD to 1700AD)

Between 800AD and 1700AD, population more than doubled from 1,15M to 2,95M (16,06 persons per 100 km²). In the Kathmandu Valley, the three Malla kingdoms engaged in intense architectural, artistic and commercial competition, expanding urban walls, constructing multi-tiered palace squares and patronising craft guilds [@Slusser1982NepalMandala; @Gosai2025Ethnograph; @Whitmarsh2022Darbar; @Glattli2021Conservati]. Kathmandu peaked at 62k residents in 1650AD (58,9k in 1700AD), Lalitpur peaked at 48k in 1650AD (43,5k in 1700AD) and Bhaktapur peaked at 40k in 1650AD (34,4k in 1700AD). Along the southeastern Duars borderland, Cooch Behar rose to 32k in 1650AD (26k in 1700AD) [@Eaton1993Rise; @Compagna2026Layered]. In the west, the Khasa Malla empire united the Karnali basin around Sinja (15,5k peak in 1300AD; 12,6k in 1200AD) before dissolving into the Baise and Chaubisi principalities [@Hutt1984Nepali]. In Bhutan, the consolidation of the Drukpa theocracy under Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal concentrated administration within fortress-monasteries at Punakha (7,5k in 1700AD), Thimphu (7k in 1700AD), Paro (6,8k in 1700AD), Jakar (6k peak in 1700AD) and Trongsa (5,1k in 1700AD) [@Phuntsho2013HistoryBhutan; @Ling2016India].

### Gorkha Unification and the Early Modern Baseline (1700AD to 1816AD)

Between 1700AD and 1816AD, regional population climbed from 2,95M to 3,65M (19,87 persons per 100 km²). Gorkha military expansion unified the central, eastern and western hills into a cohesive imperial state centred on Kathmandu [@Whitmarsh2022Darbar; @Kieniewicz2020Identifyin]. Commercial treaties with Tibet and the opening of new agricultural lands in the Morang Terai and mid-hill valleys supported growing population numbers alongside bustling frontier market towns such as Musahri (43,1k in 1816AD), Pilibhit (29,6k in 1816AD) and Rajganj (29,2k in 1816AD) [@Bayly1983Rulers; @Naqvi1968Urbanisation; @Kovacs2024Bengal; @Compagna2026Layered]. Following the Anglo-Nepalese War and the Treaty of Sugauli in 1816AD, Nepal stabilised within boundaries approximating its modern frontiers.

Across all 4.060 catalogued settlements, peak city sizes follow a well-behaved Zipf rank-size power law ($\alpha = 0,80$, $R^2 = 0,99$). The urban settlement hierarchy across the Himalayas conformed to a distinct four-tiered functional organisation:
1. Primary intramontane metropolises and major frontier cities (> 25k peak inhabitants): Kathmandu (62k peak in 1650AD; 52,8k in 1816AD), Lalitpur (48k peak in 1650AD; 31,4k in 1816AD), Shravasti (45k peak in 300BC along the southwestern Terai margin), Musahri (43,1k in 1816AD), Bhaktapur (40k peak in 1650AD; 23,4k in 1816AD), Cooch Behar (32k peak in 1650AD; 16,8k in 1816AD), Pilibhit (29,6k in 1816AD), Rajganj (29,2k in 1816AD) and Ghorahi (26,2k in 1816AD). These urban centres combined royal administration, trans-Himalayan brokerage, specialised handicraft manufacturing and sub-Himalayan market exchange [@Slusser1982NepalMandala; @Toffin1990Mythical; @Sengupta2017Ruptured; @Bayly1983Rulers].
2. Major regional centres and frontier marts (10k to 25k peak inhabitants): Bahraich (22,9k in 1816AD), Dumra (20,2k in 1816AD), Singiya (19,9k in 1816AD), Dharan (19,8k in 1816AD), Bettiah (19,8k in 1816AD), Phulwari (18,9k in 1816AD), Lahan (18,2k in 1816AD), Tilaurakot (18k peak in 300BC), Janakpur (18k peak in 300BC; 15,2k in 1816AD), Bhimdatta (16,7k in 1816AD), Sinja (15,5k peak in 1300AD) and Gorkha (11,4k peak in 1750AD; 8k in 1816AD) [@Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @Coningham2021Urban; @Naqvi1968Urbanisation].
3. Fortified provincial capitals and monastic dzongs (5k to 10k peak inhabitants): Binnaguri (9,8k in 1816AD), Alipurduar (9,6k in 1816AD), Punakha (8,5k peak in 1775AD; 8k in 1816AD), Thimphu (7,5k in 1750AD to 1816AD), Paro (7k peak in 1750AD; 6,5k in 1816AD), Jakar (6k peak in 1700AD; 5,5k in 1816AD) and Trongsa (5,5k peak in 1750AD; 5,2k in 1816AD). These fortress-monasteries coordinated agricultural tax collection and spiritual life [@Phuntsho2013HistoryBhutan; @Ling2016India].
4. Secondary religious shrines, market towns and river outposts (< 5k peak inhabitants): Piprahwa (2,6k peak in 300AD), Ramagrama (2,7k peak in 300AD) and over three thousand agrarian market villages, *qasba* nodes and mountain crossings spanning the four physiographic divisions [@Allchin1995Archaeology; @Habib1982Atlas; @Chattopadhyaya1994Making].

# Limitations

Demographic modelling across the Himalayan mountains is subject to specific methodological and taphonomic constraints:
1. High-relief taphonomic loss and seismic destruction: the active collision between the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates causes frequent high-magnitude earthquakes (such as the devastating tremors of 1255AD, 1408AD, 1681AD and 1833AD) that levelled multi-tiered brick architecture across the Kathmandu Valley and trigger catastrophic landslides on mountain slopes [@Coningham2021Urban].
2. Monsoon weathering of mud-brick and timber structures: torrential seasonal rainfall rapidly degrades unbaked earthen ramparts and wooden domestic structures outside stone-built monastic bastions, obscuring early mediaeval rural house footprints [@Gosai2025Ethnograph; @Parajuli1999Agro].
3. Heterogeneity of precolonial archival records: while Licchavi stone inscriptions and Malla land deeds provide rich data for the Kathmandu basin, documentation across the eastern Kirat hills, the western Karnali valleys and early Bhutan relies heavily on oral genealogies (*vamshavali*), monastic tax registers and retrospective British colonial intelligence reports [@Hutt1984Nepali; @Kieniewicz2020Identifyin; @Compagna2026Layered].
4. Fluid frontier delimitation in border tracts: before the Treaty of Sugauli (1816AD), sovereignty across the Terai and Duars fluctuated between hill polities and Gangetic empires (Awadh, Bengal, Koch Bihar), necessitating careful territorial harmonisation [@Kovacs2024Bengal; @Compagna2026Layered].

# Conclusion

The demographic trajectory of Nepal and Bhutan from 10000BC to 1816AD demonstrates the gradual expansion and adaptation of human societies across steep Himalayan altitudinal gradients. From sparse terminal Pleistocene foraging bands numbering 15k individuals, regional population expanded to 680k under classical Licchavi urbanisation, reaching 1,65M during the mediaeval Malla and Khasa eras and attaining 3,65M inhabitants across 183.712 km² of territory at the 1816AD baseline.

This demographic growth was anchored by three primary mechanisms: the development of intensive gravitational irrigation and multi-cropping in intramontane lacustrine basins, the expansion of trans-Himalayan commerce linking northern India with Tibet, and the political consolidation of civic institutions, notably the Newar *guthi* land trusts, the Khasa highland state and the Bhutanese Drukpa dzong administration. Following Gorkha imperial unification and the Treaty of Sugauli, the established agrarian and urban networks formed the durable structural foundation of modern Himalayan nation-states.
